entries.title: Room for their own movement
entries.invitation: The authors make room for the baby’s own awake movement, with comfort and help close by.
entries.summary: The authors favor awake movement that the baby initiates, with room to explore, help when needed, and no propping into sitting or standing before they can get there themselves.
entries.cue: Notice how your baby moves now, what catches their attention, and when effort becomes frustration.
detail: Davies and Uzodike describe a prepared space where a baby can explore their own movements. A nearby object may invite a reach or a change of direction; the point is to follow the baby’s present interest and pace.

Their caution is about propping a baby into sitting or standing. They separately describe awake time on both the back and tummy, while noticing discomfort and changing things or picking the baby up when needed.

When effort turns to frustration, they describe coming closer and offering enough help for the baby to continue. Their activity ages are guides, and they explicitly welcome seeking support for developmental concerns.

entries.title: Learning to use a fork, spoon and glass
entries.summary: The books describe letting a child take over parts of eating as coordination grows, with small, manageable tools and adult help. Food and cutlery stay at the table.
entries.cue: Your child is interested in bringing a utensil or glass to their mouth during a meal.
detail: In The Montessori Baby, an adult puts food on a fork and leaves the handle toward the baby, who chooses a hand and lifts it. The adult refills it and waits for the baby to continue. Their examples use short, baby-sized handles and fork prongs that are not too sharp.

For a spoon, both books describe thicker foods such as oatmeal while the child is learning to keep food on it. The Baby book also describes a little water in a small glass, with an adult helping support it as needed. Low-sided bowls make the food easier to reach.

The Baby authors favor real dishes but also acknowledge breakage and give less breakable alternatives while a baby is experimenting with dropping. Material choice alone does not show that a dish or utensil suits this child.

Davies gives a similar fork-and-spoon example for young toddlers. Her toddler guidance keeps food and forks at the table and requires supervision for activities involving sharp objects or small parts. Her eating chapter also directs families with eating concerns to a doctor.

These examples sit within each book’s account of eating at the child’s own pace. The Baby book places solids after six months and signs of readiness, alongside choking precautions and learning first aid; its fork examples are not a deadline for using cutlery.

entries.title: When your baby hits, bites, pushes or throws
entries.summary: When a baby hits, bites, pushes or throws, the authors look for what the movement might communicate while keeping a kind, clear limit on hurting. The adult helps when feelings are too strong for words.
entries.cue: Your baby is showing a strong preference through their movements, and someone or something may be hurt.
detail: The book describes some babies showing stronger preferences around nine to twelve months. A hit might follow unwanted handling; a push might mean wanting to get past. A bite might come with hunger, upset or teething. These are questions to consider, not certain explanations.

Throwing can be a different kind of exploration: the object may be too easy or difficult, or the baby may be interested in how it falls. The authors look for another way to explore that is not dangerous or disruptive. Their boundaries chapter gives a basket of suitable balls as one alternative to throwing an unsuitable object.

The adult stops hurtful actions and can move with the baby away from the situation when needed. During intense crying, the authors use few words, offer a cuddle if wanted and stay nearby if touch is refused.

After calm returns, they give a short explanation and model repair, such as offering a tissue to someone who was hurt or putting thrown things back. They describe babies watching this before taking more of a part as toddlers.
For repeated situations, the book looks at what happened just before, including noise, crowding, a difficult transition or an activity’s fit. Adjusting those conditions is another way to help.

entries.summary: Davies suggests returning to repeated nighttime requests at a calm daytime moment. The adult and child can think together about what might help, while keeping the child’s need for support in view.

entries.title: A ring off, a ring on
entries.summary: The books describe taking rings off a post before finding a way to put them back. Repeating one small movement can be the whole activity, with adult supervision, materials suitable for mouthing, appropriate sizes and secure parts.

Later Baby examples use a basket with two or three rings and a peg at 10–12+ months, then two or three same-size napkin rings on a spindle at 11–12+ months. These offer different ways to repeat taking off and putting on; they are not a shopping list.

Both appendices list four or five rings of different sizes from 12+ months. The Baby chapter also describes horizontal and curved posts; the Toddler appendix places those variants around 14–16 months, and three colored pegs with rings at 15–18+ months.
